passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking so persistently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. The makers appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘There is one who said to his own wisdom, “Let us make a human.” Wisdom, with which he himself always rejoiced as with his own spirit, is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand, creating the whole. For this reason one human also came into being, and from him the female came forth. Though one in kind, it is a pair. For through extension and contraction the one is considered two. Thus I act rightly in rendering all honor to one God as to parents.’ Simon said, ‘What then? Even if the scriptures speak of other gods, will you not accept them?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥνωται μὲν ὡς ψυχὴ τῷ θεῷ, ἐκτείνεται δὲ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ὡς χείρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both soul and hand comparisons are retained as the author's own account of wisdom. The rendering does not convert these comparisons into a later creedal definition or a separate independent creator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ μία οὖσα τῷ γένει δυάς ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Though one in kind, it is a pair
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine one and the noun pair can concern the human kind represented by male and female, with a possible continuing analogy to wisdom. The English leaves the collective referent broad instead of introducing a second named divine person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ γὰρ ἔκτασιν καὶ συστολὴν ἡ μονὰς δυὰς εἶναι νομίζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For through extension and contraction the one is considered two
lexical_decisions.rationale: The numerical unity and duality are translated into accessible English while preserving both spatial-process terms. A unit is considered a pair is a more technical alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to one God as to parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular one God and plural parents are both retained. The comparison is not silently normalized to one parent or expanded into two gods.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything, would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand, as can be shown from many passages. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we can neither be made to stumble by scriptures or anyone else, nor be deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.
The repeated testing root is retained, with tempter distinguishing the agent from God in Peter's stated argument. The noun is not silently replaced by a personal name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and the one who wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves the pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving that attachment silently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

passages.text: When Simon heard this, he said, ‘Since you say that one must not believe even a prophet who gives signs and wonders but speaks of another god, knowing that he also deserves death, then your teacher too, who gave signs and wonders, was reasonably put to death.’ Peter answered, ‘Our Lord neither declared that gods exist besides the one who created everything nor proclaimed himself to be God. But he reasonably pronounced blessed the person who said that he was the son of the God who ordered everything.’ Simon answered, ‘Does it not seem to you, then, that one who comes from God is God?’ Peter said, ‘Tell us how this can be. We cannot tell you this, because we did not hear it from him.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: nor proclaimed himself to be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The denial is retained as the author's Peter states it. It is not corrected or softened to conform to a denominational account of Christ's identity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one who comes from God is God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The origin phrase is rendered openly. God versus a god is a material English article alternative; the Greek argument concerns application of the divine designation rather than a newly specified rank in a pantheon.
